Each chapter section has the same five parts: the chapter's setting in the sequence, close readings of specific verses, connections to Jesus Christ with the textual reasons for them, cross-references, and questions. How to use this guide
This guide is meant for adults who want to read Isaiah slowly. Each chapter section has the same five parts: the chapter's setting in the sequence, close readings of specific verses, connections to Jesus Christ with the textual reasons for them, cross-references, and questions. Most of the work is reading the King James text closely. Secondary sources are used sparingly and named when they appear.
The guide tries to keep three kinds of statement separate:

What the text states. Isaiah's words, quoted from the King James Version and cited by verse.
What a commentator argues. Each of these is attributed in the sentence and linked.
Proposed devotional application. These are marked as application. They are offered for reflection, not as the meaning the text requires.



Historical orientation
Isaiah 39 ends with a warning. After King Hezekiah shows his treasures to envoys from Babylon, Isaiah tells him that "all that is in thine house... shall be carried to Babylon" and that some of his descendants will serve in the Babylonian palace (Isaiah 39:6–7). Then the voice changes. Chapter 40 opens with "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people." Judgment has dominated much of the book up to this point. Now the speech is addressed to a people living after the catastrophe.
The historical frame is approximately the following:

Late 600s BC. Babylon replaced Assyria as the dominant power.
597 and 586 BC. Babylonian armies deported Judah's leaders. In 586 they destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple.
539 BC. Cyrus the Persian took Babylon.
Soon after. His decree allowed exiles to return and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1–4; compare 2 Chronicles 36:22–23).

Isaiah 40–49 speaks to people facing that reality. Their city is in ruins. They live under a foreign empire with impressive gods and processions. Many of them suspect their own God has forgotten them (40:27; 49:14).
Readers handle authorship differently. Many biblical scholars attribute chapters 40–55 to a later prophet writing during the exile. Latter-day Saints have generally read these chapters as Isaiah's prophecy. One reason is that Nephi, around 600 BC, quotes Isaiah 48–49 from the brass plates (1 Nephi 20–21). Readers on either view can agree on the setting the chapters address: exile in Babylon and the hope of return. This guide reads the chapters within that setting first, then follows how later scripture applies them.
The official lesson, Come, Follow Me—For Home and Church: Old Testament 2026, frames these chapters as a turn toward comfort for Jews facing the loss of Jerusalem and captivity, and it extends that hope to present readers. The lesson also acknowledges that "servant" passages can refer to Jesus Christ, to Israel, or to Cyrus. It points readers to 1 Nephi 22 to see how Nephi and Jacob likened Isaiah 48–49, and it invites readers to ponder 48:10 alongside 49:13–16.
Taylor Halverson's Interpreter Foundation study, "'Besides Me There is No Saviour.' Isaiah 40–49", reads the block by asking what each portrait teaches about God's character. His examples include God as unique Savior, refiner, shepherd, teacher, and covenant-keeper. That question helps here. These chapters argue about God. The argument centers on whether Israel's God can be trusted when Babylon appears to have won.

Christian reading finds Jesus Christ most clearly in the servant poems, especially 42:1–7 and 49:1–7, because the New Testament reads them that way. That reading does not erase Israel's own vocation. It also does not make Cyrus a type of Christ in any simple sense.

runs.text: , comfort spoken "to the heart."

The KJV's "Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem" introduces three declarations. Her "warfare is accomplished," her "iniquity is pardoned," and she "hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins." The text frames the exile as covenant judgment. That framing belongs to Israel's prophetic interpretation of a national catastrophe.

runs.text: The word "double" should not be turned into a precise heavenly ledger in which Jerusalem paid twice what she owed. The text gives no arithmetic. Its point is that the time of judgment is complete and nothing more is outstanding. Isaiah later uses "double" in the opposite direction: "For your shame ye shall have double... everlasting joy shall be unto them" (

runs.text: , a highway for God.

The voice does not say "prepare a way for yourselves." It says "Prepare ye the way of the LORD... a highway for our God." The return from exile is pictured as God's own procession. Valleys are lifted and mountains lowered so "the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together." Exiles who once walked east in chains now see a road leveled for their God to lead them home. The image echoes the Exodus without repeating it: once the way led through the sea, and now it runs across the desert.

runs.text: , grass and the word.

The second voice says "Cry," and the prophet asks, "What shall I cry?" The answer is unflattering: "All flesh is grass." Babylon is grass. So is Israel ("surely the people is grass"). Only "the word of our God shall stand for ever." This is the chapter's first argument. Empires are seasonal, and God's promise is not.

previewRoot.text:
Seeing Jesus Christ in the chapter
The New Testament explicitly applies 40:3 to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:3; John 1:23). Luke extends the quotation through "all flesh shall see the salvation of God" (Luke 3:4–6). In Isaiah the way is prepared for "the LORD... our God." So when the Gospels apply it to Jesus, they identify Jesus with the coming of Israel's God.
The shepherd of 40:11 anticipates Jesus's self-description as the good shepherd (John 10:11). Peter quotes 40:6–8 and then adds, "this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you" (1 Peter 1:24–25).

runs.text: Questions for study and discussion
Verse 2 makes three declarations about Jerusalem. Which of them does the chapter develop most, and why might the order matter?
Verses 10 and 11 both describe God's arm. What does each picture contribute, and what would be lost if you kept only one?
Verse 7 says "surely the people is grass." How does including Israel among the grass change the message from "Babylon will fall" into something more searching?
The complaint in
is answered mostly with statements about who God is, not with an explanation of events. Is that a satisfying answer? Why or why not?
In what kinds of experiences is walking without fainting harder than mounting up as eagles?

Chapter 41 turns the argument of chapter 40 into a trial scene. The islands and peoples are summoned to "come near together to judgment" (

). Two linked questions run through the chapter. Who controls history? And who can explain it beforehand? In the middle of the trial God turns to Israel with some of the most tender promises in these chapters.

The prophet's diagnosis is not stupidity. It is a deceived heart. The idolater cannot make the simple inventory that would expose the absurdity. The same block of wood cannot be fuel and savior at once.
Application:

The modern equivalent is seldom carved wood. It is anything we make or acquire with our own hands and then ask to deliver us, such as money, reputation, or a political cause. runs.text: , the anointed king who does not know God.

"Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden." The word "anointed" was used for Israel's kings and priests. Calling a Persian ruler "anointed" means he is commissioned by God for a specific task. God will "go before thee," "break in pieces the gates of brass," and give "the treasures of darkness" (

previewRoot.text: 45:1–4, the anointed king who does not know God. "Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden." The word "anointed" was used for Israel's kings and priests. Calling a Persian ruler "anointed" means he is commissioned by God for a specific task. God will "go before thee," "break in pieces the gates of brass," and give "the treasures of darkness" (45:2–3).

runs.text: Two purposes are given. The first is "that thou mayest know that I, the LORD... am the God of Israel" (
). The second, and more basic, is "For Jacob my servant's sake, and Israel mine elect" (
). Cyrus is not the servant here. Jacob is the servant, and Cyrus is commissioned for Jacob's sake.
The phrase "though thou hast not known me" appears twice (
). God works through Cyrus whether or not Cyrus acknowledges him.

Cyrus is not Jesus. He is a historical ruler whose victories served God's purposes for Israel. The text never presents him as a redeemer from sin, a sufferer, or a covenant figure. It does show that God's sovereignty reaches beyond his covenant people.
Application:

That idea brings comfort and also humility. God can work through institutions and people who do not acknowledge him. The text does not make every powerful person God's chosen instrument, and it does not ask readers to endorse every ruler.

runs.text: Setting in the sequence

Chapter 46 is short and tightly built. It begins with Babylon's gods being hauled away on animals. It contrasts them with the God who has carried Israel from birth. Then it returns to the argument from foreknowledge and the "ravenous bird from the east."

"Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth, their idols were upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast." Bel was a title of Marduk, Babylon's chief god, and Nebo (Nabu) was another major Babylonian deity.

title.text: The fall of the lady of kingdoms

runs.text: Setting in the sequence

Chapter 47 is a taunt song over Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem. Babylon is personified as a pampered royal woman forced off her throne. The chapter is the counterpart to chapter 49, where desolate Zion, also personified as a woman, is restored. These two women frame the end of the block.

previewRoot.text:
Setting in the sequence
Chapter 47 is a taunt song over Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem. Babylon is personified as a pampered royal woman forced off her throne. The chapter is the counterpart to chapter 49, where desolate Zion, also personified as a woman, is restored. These two women frame the end of the block.

runs.text: Reading with care

This chapter uses the imagery of conquest: a woman stripped, humiliated, and widowed. In the ancient world, conquered cities and especially their women actually suffered such things. The text personifies an empire. It does not command anyone to humiliate real people, and it should never be used to justify degrading anyone. The chapter is prophetic judgment against an imperial power, voiced for a people that power had crushed.
Readers can acknowledge that the imagery is painful. They can also recognize that for exiles, hearing the oppressor's fall announced was an act of hope.

runs.text: Synthesis

Isaiah 40–49 begins with a command to comfort and ends with Zion's children gathering and "all flesh" coming to know her Redeemer. Between those points, the chapters sustain one argument. Babylon looked like it had won. Its gods were carried in procession, its experts read the stars, and its queen said "I am, and none else." Israel was blind, deaf, burned, and afraid that its way was hidden from God.
The prophet answers with several claims:
God is incomparable (chapters 40, 46).
He alone foretells and directs history, even through a Persian king who does not know him (41, 44–45).
He remains present in the waters and the fire (43).
He refines rather than destroys (48).
He remembers Zion more faithfully than a mother remembers her child (49).
Three cautions emerge from close reading.
"Servant" names more than one figure.

The word applies to Israel in its calling and in its blindness, to a prophet, and to a figure who restores Israel and enlightens the nations. The New Testament recognizes that last figure in Jesus. Cyrus is a commissioned ruler, not a redeemer.
The promises do not guarantee an easy life.
Isaiah 43:2
assumes waters and fire. Daniel's friends and Abinadi show that God's faithfulness can mean rescue or resurrection.
Judgment language is not a license.
Babylon's fall is God's judgment on a merciless empire. It gives no permission to humiliate anyone. Israel's exile, read as judgment, does not make every sufferer guilty.
Within those cautions, the Christ-centered reading is well supported. The New Testament identifies Jesus with the coming LORD of

. Latter-day Saint scripture adds that the Holy One who says "beside me there is no saviour" is Jesus Christ. It also adds that the hands which remember Zion bear the prints of nails.
Application:

The chapters do not ask readers to pretend that exile was not exile. They ask readers to wait upon the Lord, to bear witness while their own sight is still being healed, and to trust a God who carries his people from the womb to old age.

Synthesis
Isaiah 40–49 begins with a command to comfort and ends with Zion's children gathering and "all flesh" coming to know her Redeemer. Between those points, the chapters sustain one argument. Babylon looked like it had won. Its gods were carried in procession, its experts read the stars, and its queen said "I am, and none else." Israel was blind, deaf, burned, and afraid that its way was hidden from God.
The prophet answers with several claims:

God is incomparable (chapters 40, 46).
He alone foretells and directs history, even through a Persian king who does not know him (41, 44–45).
He remains present in the waters and the fire (43).
He refines rather than destroys (48).
He remembers Zion more faithfully than a mother remembers her child (49).

"Servant" names more than one figure. The word applies to Israel in its calling and in its blindness, to a prophet, and to a figure who restores Israel and enlightens the nations. The New Testament recognizes that last figure in Jesus. Cyrus is a commissioned ruler, not a redeemer.

The world these chapters imagine
Isaiah 50–57 speaks into a world of exile and return. Jerusalem fell to Babylon in the early sixth century before Christ. Many Latter-day Saints affirm the eighth-century Isaiah as author. One reason is that Book of Mormon writers before Christ quote substantial portions of Isaiah 48–53, though not every verse: Isaiah 48–49 in 1 Nephi 20–21, Isaiah 50–51 and 52:1–2 in 2 Nephi 7–8, Isaiah 52:7–10 in Mosiah 12 and 15, and Isaiah 53 in Mosiah 14. The Book of Mormon presents its Isaiah material as words its writers had from the brass plates, which Lehi's family carried from Jerusalem around 600 BC. Isaiah 54 is quoted only later, by the resurrected Jesus in 3 Nephi 22. That quotation does not by itself show that Isaiah 54 was on the brass plates. This guide does not need to settle that debate. Either way, the text deliberately speaks to exiles and returnees. Its images come from that experience: debt slavery, divorce, prison, ruined walls, a long road home, temple vessels carried back, and a community arguing about who belongs.

These eight chapters move in recognizable stages.

Then comes the long poem that begins at 52:13 and runs through 53:12. The chapter break inherited from medieval Bible divisions obscures this. The poem should be read as one unit across the chapter boundary. The Hebrew does not label its speakers, so any division into voices is a reconstruction. A common and plausible reading hears three voices. God appears to speak first (52:13–15). A group calling itself "we" then seems to confess how badly it misjudged the servant (roughly 53:1–10a). Who the "we" are is debated. God's voice then seems to return to vindicate the servant through 53:12. Some readers place that return at 53:10b, and others at 53:11 ("my righteous servant").
Chapter 54 turns to the city as a once-barren mother whose tent must now expand. Chapter 55 is an invitation to a free feast and an everlasting covenant.
With chapter 56 the tone changes. The audience now seems to be a community back in the land, wrestling with Sabbath, temple, and membership. Foreigners and eunuchs are promised a place, while careless leaders are condemned. The word "servant" carries many meanings in Isaiah. Israel or Jacob is explicitly called God's servant (41:8–9; 44:1–2; 49:3). The speaker changes abruptly to "me." This first-person speaker is the subject of the third servant song.

is built around a pairing: the "tongue" and the "ear" of "the learned." The Hebrew word behind "learned" means a disciple or one who has been taught. The same word appears in

("my disciples"). The speaker can speak well because he has first been taught. The purpose of his speech is not display but help: "to speak a word in season to him that is weary." The weary person needs a timely word, and the speaker's skill exists for that person.

title.text: Back, cheek, and face

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 50:6 — Back, cheek, and face

runs.text: "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting."

This verse describes abuse in three parts, and in each part the speaker's own action comes first. "I gave," "I hid not." The servant's back is struck. His beard is torn, the "hair" of the cheeks, which in Israelite culture was an act of extreme humiliation (compare
2 Samuel 10:4–5
, where shaving half of the envoys' beards is a grave insult). His face receives spit.

The grammar matters. The servant is not described as passive in the sense of helpless. He chose not to avoid the consequences of his obedience in verse 5. The suffering follows from faithfulness, not from guilt.
Matthew 26:67
records that Jesus was spat upon and struck during his trial before the council. The parallel is close.
Matthew 27:26–31

adds scourging and further mockery by soldiers. One honest limit: no Gospel describes Jesus's beard being plucked. The correspondence is strong but not total. The Gospels do not quote this verse as a formal fulfillment text. The connection rests on the pattern and on Christianity's wider reading of the servant songs as a whole.

One more caution. The servant "gave" his back. That does not mean anyone who is abused is being called to offer their back. The verse describes a specific act of costly faithfulness in a prophetic mission. It is not a rule for people facing violence at home or elsewhere. Seeking safety does not contradict this text.

Verse 7

turns from what was done to the servant to what he expects. "The Lord GOD will help me." The verb is future, though often read with present force. Because of that expected help, he will not be "confounded," that is, disgraced. The face that was spat upon in verse 6 is now "set ... like a flint." Flint is an exceptionally hard stone, and the prophet uses it as an image of a face fixed in unyielding resolve. The image is not of a man who feels nothing. It is of a man whose direction cannot be shifted.
Luke 9:51
uses similar language: Jesus "stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." Luke does not cite
Isaiah 50
, but the shared image of a determined face is a meaningful thematic link.
Verse 8

introduces the courtroom. "He is near that justifieth me; who will contend with me? let us stand together: who is mine adversary? let him come near to me." "Justify" here is legal: to declare someone in the right. The judge who will acquit the servant is "near," and in that confidence the servant invites any accuser to bring charges. "Let us stand together" means let us stand up together in court.
Verse 9

completes the legal sequence. "Behold, the Lord GOD will help me; who is he that shall condemn me? lo, they all shall wax old as a garment; the moth shall eat them up." The accusers do not last. Like a garment eaten by moths, their power decays. The same moth image returns in
Romans 8:33–34

Paul applies the servant's courtroom confidence to everyone in Christ. Because Christ died, rose, and intercedes, no accusation can finally stand against those who belong to him.
Paul's use stays close to Isaiah's logic. He does not deny that accusers exist. He denies that their charges can finally stand when God is the one who justifies.

A further caution: this passage does not promise that faithful people avoid accusation or suffering. The servant has already been beaten in verse 6. Vindication follows suffering; it does not prevent it.

Romans 8:33–34 closely resembles these verses: "Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth?" Paul applies the servant's courtroom confidence to everyone in Christ. Because Christ died, rose, and intercedes, no accusation can finally stand against those who belong to him.

runs.text: Isaiah 50:10
— The faithful person who walks in darkness

title.text: The faithful person who walks in darkness

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 50:10 — The faithful person who walks in darkness

runs.text: "Who is among you that feareth the LORD, that obeyeth the voice of his servant, that walketh in darkness, and hath no light? let him trust in the name of the LORD, and stay upon his God."

This may be one of the most pastorally important verses in the chapter. The person described is faithful. They fear the Lord and obey the servant's voice. Yet they walk "in darkness" and have "no light." Isaiah does not treat this person's darkness as evidence of disobedience. He describes a reverent, obedient person who still cannot see.

The counsel is not to manufacture light. It is to "trust in the name of the LORD, and stay upon his God." To "stay" means to lean on, or to be supported by. The image is of leaning one's weight on something one cannot see clearly.

The servant himself provides the model. In verses 6–9 he endured abuse without being able to see his vindication yet. He relied on the God who "will help." The faithful listener of verse 10 is invited to the same posture.

This verse preserves room for lament. It does not tell the reader to be cheerful in the dark, or to explain the darkness, or to claim it will soon lift. It simply names the condition and offers somewhere to lean.
Psalm 88
, which ends in darkness without resolution, shows that scripture can hold faithful people in unresolved trouble.

runs.text: Isaiah 50:11
— Living by sparks one has lit

title.text: Living by sparks one has lit

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 50:11 — Living by sparks one has lit

runs.text: "Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, that compass yourselves about with sparks: walk in the light of your fire, and in the sparks that ye have kindled. This shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow."

The contrast with verse 10 is direct. Some people in darkness respond by lighting their own fires and surrounding themselves with sparks. The verse then grants their wish with irony: "walk in the light of your fire." The result, given "of mine hand," is to "lie down in sorrow."

The verse should not be read as a ban on human effort, planning, or practical problem-solving. Isaiah elsewhere commends wise action. The issue is the substitution of self-made light for trust in God. In context, the self-lit fire probably represents trust in other powers, idols, or political schemes, which Isaiah regularly mocks (compare
, where a man cooks dinner and makes a god from the same wood).

Sparks give little light and burn out quickly. People who rely on them end up where they began, in darkness, now with the added sorrow of failed self-reliance. Verse 10 offers no fire at all, only a name to trust. That is harder, and Isaiah says it is safer.

runs.text: Chapter orientation

Chapter 51 is a sequence of summons. "Hearken" appears in verses 1, 4, and 7. "Awake, awake" appears in verses 9 and 17. The urgent repetitions set the pace of the chapter. Isaiah first calls the faithful to look back at Abraham and Sarah. He then turns to God himself and calls on God's arm to wake as in the days of the Exodus. Finally he calls Jerusalem to wake from a drunken stupor caused by the cup of God's wrath. The chapter ends with the cup taken away and given to the oppressors.
The Book of Mormon includes this chapter in
2 Nephi 8

, continuing Jacob's reading. There are several textual differences, noted below where relevant. Like chapter 50, chapter 51 addresses people who feel forgotten. Its answer combines memory, cosmic power, and justice.

title.text: The rock and the quarry

runs.text: "Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged." (
Verse 1

addresses not the whole nation but a narrower group: "ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD." These are the faithful, perhaps discouraged by their small numbers. The image is a quarry. A building stone is cut from the rock face, and the pit left behind shows where it came from. Isaiah tells the faithful to look back at their origin.
Verse 2

explains: "Look unto Abraham your father, and unto Sarah that bare you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him." Sarah appears by name alongside Abraham. This is rare in the prophets and significant here. Abraham was the rock and Sarah was the quarry. The two of them together are the origin of the people.
Sarah's story especially fits the exiles. She was barren for decades and laughed at the promise of a son (
Genesis 18:12
; 21:6–7). In chapter 54 the barren mother is Zion herself. Isaiah is preparing that image here.

The phrase "I called him alone" makes the point clear. God's work began with a single man and a barren woman. If God could build a people from one couple, he can rebuild Zion from a small remnant. The faithful minority should not measure their prospects by their present size.

describes the problem in detail: "And forgettest the LORD thy maker, that hath stretched forth the heavens, and laid the foundations of the earth; and hast feared continually every day because of the fury of the oppressor, as if he were ready to destroy? and where is the fury of the oppressor?"

The people's fear is not imaginary. Babylon was a real oppressor. Isaiah's point is about proportion. Constant fear of a mortal tyrant has crowded out memory of the Creator. The closing question, "where is the fury of the oppressor?", anticipates a moment when the empire's power will be gone.
Verse 14

is concrete. "The captive exile hasteneth that he may be loosed, and that he should not die in the pit, nor that his bread should fail." The prisoner is bowed down and fears dying in a pit and going hungry. The promise is release and food. Divine comfort here is not only an inner feeling. It includes freedom from prison and enough to eat.

This is an important balance in the chapter. The text does not tell people in danger that their fear is spiritual failure. It names danger as danger, then sets God's power and faithfulness against it. Reading these verses as a rebuke to the frightened would misunderstand them. They are a promise to the frightened.

title.text: The cup taken away and given to the tormentors

previewRoot.text:
Isaiah 51:21–23 — The cup taken away and given to the tormentors
Verse 21: "Therefore hear now this, thou afflicted, and drunken, but not with wine." Jerusalem's staggering is caused by suffering, not wine. The city is addressed with sympathy as "afflicted."

runs.text: Verse 22

reverses the judgment. "Thus saith thy Lord the LORD, and thy God that pleadeth the cause of his people, Behold, I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling, even the dregs of the cup of my fury; thou shalt no more drink it again." The phrase "pleadeth the cause of his people" returns to courtroom language. God now acts as Jerusalem's defense advocate. The cup is removed with a promise of finality: "no more."
Verse 23

completes the reversal. "But I will put it into the hand of them that afflict thee; which have said to thy soul, Bow down, that we may go over: and thou hast laid thy body as the ground, and as the street, to them that went over." The oppressors had forced Jerusalem to lie down so they could walk on her back, an ancient practice of humiliating conquered peoples. Now they must drink the cup.

Two things should be said about this verse. First, it is a matter of justice, not personal revenge. God, not Jerusalem, transfers the cup. The text gives no license for the oppressed to inflict cruelty in turn. Second, it insists that redemption is not merely inner calm. People who have been crushed are not told simply to feel better. The structures of oppression are dismantled. God's comfort includes justice.

Chapter 51 does not mention a servant who suffers, and the New Testament does not quote it as a prophecy of Jesus. The connection to Christ is more indirect but still real. First, verses 9–11 call on the "arm of the LORD" to wake and redeem. In
the "arm of the LORD" is revealed in the servant himself. Christian readers see the answer to

Second, the image of the cup carries into the Gospels. In Gethsemane Jesus prays that "this cup" might pass (
Matthew 26:39
Mark 14:36
). In
Doctrine and Covenants 19:18

Why might verse 2 name Sarah alongside Abraham? How does her story prepare the reader for chapter 54?

Verse 8: "Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the LORD shall bring again Zion." The watchmen on Jerusalem's walls see the runner and then see what he announces: the Lord returning to Zion.

runs.text: The phrase "eye to eye" in English often means agreement of opinion. In Hebrew it is closer to "with their own eyes," that is, seeing directly, face to face (compare
Numbers 14:14

, where the Lord is "seen face to face," literally "eye to eye"). The watchmen sing together because they all witness the same thing. Shared sight produces shared song. Latter-day Saint usage sometimes uses "see eye to eye" for unity of understanding. That is a meaningful application, but the verse's primary point is eyewitness seeing.
Verse 9

: "Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the LORD hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem." Even the ruins are called to sing. The verbs are in the past tense: God "hath comforted," "hath redeemed." This is the Hebrew prophetic perfect, which describes a certain future as though it had already happened.
Verse 10

: "The LORD hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God." A warrior rolled up his sleeve to fight. God's arm, called upon in
, is now bared. The audience expands: "all the nations" and "all the ends of the earth" will see this salvation. Zion's restoration is meant to be public and universal.

runs.text: Chapter orientation
This chapter is the center of the week's reading and continues the poem begun at
. The Hebrew does not mark speakers, so the following divisions are a common, plausible reconstruction rather than a settled fact. On that reading, God speaks in
. A group calling itself "we" then speaks through roughly
, confessing its earlier misjudgment of the servant. God's voice returns at
or
and continues through
Who is the "we"? Several answers are possible. It may be the kings and nations of

, who have now come to understand. It may be Israel, or a part of Israel, confessing its failure to recognize the servant. In the Christian reading, it is everyone who confesses that Christ's suffering was for them. The text does not fix the answer. Readers have found each of these meaningful.
Donald W. Parry, in "The Messiah in Isaiah 53: Four Recurring Themes," organizes the chapter around four themes:
the servant's suffering;
his bearing of others' burdens;
his death;
his vindication and reward.
These four groupings are Parry's (
Parry, "The Messiah in Isaiah 53"

). This guide uses them as a theological synthesis rather than only a checklist of fulfilled predictions. That use is this guide's editorial application, not a claim about Parry's own view. In this guide's reading, the themes interweave through the poem rather than appearing in neat sequence.
In the Book of Mormon, Abinadi quotes the entire chapter to Noah's priests (Mosiah 14). One modern scholarly proposal about how Mosiah uses the chapter is noted briefly at verse 11.

runs.text: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not."
The word "despised" begins and ends the verse, framing it. Between those two words is the servant's experience.

"A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief": the Hebrew words translated "sorrows" and "grief" include physical pain and sickness. The phrase "acquainted with" uses a verb meaning to know intimately. The servant was familiar with pain and sickness in a personal, experiential way.

The response of the "we" is the most painful part of the verse: "we hid as it were our faces from him." This is how people sometimes react to the severely ill or disfigured, looking away from what is hard to see. "We esteemed him not" sums up their judgment: the servant was of no account.
This is the beginning of a confession. The speakers do not describe the servant's suffering from a safe distance. They confess their own failure to see him. In
Isaiah 53
understanding the servant requires admitting that one first misjudged him.

title.text: The great reversal

runs.text: "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted."
This verse turns the poem. The first word, "Surely," marks a discovery. The griefs and sorrows that the servant knew in verse 3 were
ours
. He did not just know grief. He carried our grief, as one carries a heavy load.

The second half of the verse confesses the earlier misjudgment. "We did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted." Ancient people often assumed that severe suffering meant divine punishment for the sufferer's own sin. Job's friends assumed this. Jesus's disciples assumed it about the man born blind (
John 9:2
). The speakers assumed it about the servant. Verse 4 is the moment that assumption collapses. The servant was not suffering for his own sins. He was carrying theirs.

This reversal has a pastoral corollary. If the speakers were wrong to assume the servant's suffering proved God's rejection, readers should be cautious about drawing the same conclusion about any sufferer.
Isaiah 53
gives no support to the idea that suffering is a sign of guilt. It explicitly confesses that that idea was wrong in the servant's case.

quotes this verse in the context of Jesus's healing ministry: "Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses." Matthew applies it to healing of disease and demon possession, not only to the cross. This reflects the range of the Hebrew words. The servant bears pain and sickness as well as sin.

Alma reads the servant's burden-bearing as the basis for Christ's understanding and compassion. Alma 7 does not say that every sufferer will discover why they suffer. It says that the Savior knows their suffering from the inside.

— Wounded for us, straying all of us

title.text: Wounded for us, straying all of us

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 53:5–6 — Wounded for us, straying all of us

runs.text: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." (
Verse 5
expands the reversal through a series of contrasts. In each clause, the servant receives suffering and the "we" receive the benefit:
he was wounded, for our transgressions;
he was bruised, for our iniquities;
the chastisement was upon him, for our peace;
the stripes were his, and we are healed.
"Wounded" is a strong word that can mean pierced. "Bruised" means crushed. "Chastisement" means discipline or correction. "Stripes" are the welts of blows. The images are concrete, physical violence.

The verse draws on several frameworks at once. Wounding and healing are medical images. Chastisement and peace come from a framework of discipline and reconciliation. Transgressions and iniquities belong to legal and covenant language. Isaiah does not explain how the servant's suffering heals others. He gives multiple images, each adding a dimension. Christian theology has developed various models of atonement from these images. The text itself is richer than any single model.
John 19:1
records that Pilate had Jesus scourged, a concrete instance of the "stripes" this verse names.
1 Peter 2:24
quotes the verse directly: "by whose stripes ye were healed."
"All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all." (
Verse 6

begins and ends with "all." "All we" went astray, and the Lord laid on the servant "the iniquity of us all." Between these two "alls" is the image of sheep scattering, each wandering in its own direction. Sin is described here not only as rebellion but as wandering, a loss of direction that is both collective and individual.

The final clause, "the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all," introduces God as the actor. This raises a theological question addressed more fully at verse 10. For now, notice that the verse places God's action within a story of human straying. The servant does not suffer because God is arbitrary. He bears the consequences of human wandering.
1 Peter 2:25
completes the image: "For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls." The straying sheep of
Isaiah 53:6
find their way back to the one who bore their iniquity.

runs.text: Isaiah 53:7
— Silent like a lamb

title.text: Silent like a lamb

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 53:7 — Silent like a lamb

runs.text: "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth."
The sheep image from verse 6 continues, but with a reversal. In verse 6, "we" were the sheep, wandering. In verse 7, the servant is a sheep led to slaughter and a ewe before shearers, silent.
"He opened not his mouth" appears twice, framing the verse. The servant does not protest, threaten, or retaliate.
The Gospels record Jesus's silence before his accusers. Mark 14:60–61: "he held his peace, and answered nothing."
Matthew 26:63

records the same silence before the high priest. Jesus's silence is not total. He speaks at points during his trials. His silence is a refusal to defend himself in ways that would obstruct the course he had chosen.
is the most explicit New Testament reading of this verse. An Ethiopian official is reading
Isaiah 53:7–8

in his chariot. He asks Philip whether the prophet speaks of himself or someone else. Philip "began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus." The quotation in Acts follows the ancient Greek translation, so its wording differs from the KJV of Isaiah. The Ethiopian's question, "of whom speaketh the prophet this?", is the same question this guide has kept in view. Philip's answer is the Christian one.

A crucial caution: Jesus's silence before unjust accusers was a specific, voluntary act tied to his unique mission. It is not a model for people suffering abuse. The verse must never be used to tell someone being harmed to stay quiet, endure, or refrain from seeking help or justice.

Nothing in Isaiah or the gospel requires victims to remain silent. Indeed, the servant poem itself is an act of speaking up about an injustice that others failed to see.

runs.text: Isaiah 53:8
— Taken away by an unjust process

title.text: Taken away by an unjust process

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 53:8 — Taken away by an unjust process

runs.text: "He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken."

This verse is notoriously difficult in Hebrew, and translations vary widely. "Taken from prison and from judgment" may mean taken away by oppression and legal process, that is, by an unjust trial. "Who shall declare his generation?" is ambiguous:
It may mean "who could imagine his future descendants," since he was cut off with no children.
It may mean "who among his generation considered" what was happening to him.
It may mean "who can describe his life story."

"Cut off out of the land of the living" is a clear reference to death. "For the transgression of my people was he stricken" repeats the substitution theme. The phrase "my people" may shift to God's voice or may still be the community speaking.
Acts 8:33

quotes this verse in its Greek form: "In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: and who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth." Philip applies it to Jesus's unjust trial and death.
In
Mosiah 15:10–13

, Abinadi takes up the question of the servant's "generation" through verse 10's promise that he "shall see his seed." His seed, Abinadi says, are the prophets and all who have hearkened to their words and looked forward to redemption. The one "cut off" without natural descendants has a vast spiritual posterity.

runs.text: Isaiah 53:9
— An innocent man's grave

title.text: An innocent man's grave

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 53:9 — An innocent man's grave

runs.text: "And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth."

The servant is buried among the wicked and the rich. In Hebrew poetry the two may be parallel, with "the rich" meaning those who enrich themselves by oppression. Or they may contrast, with the servant assigned a criminal's grave but ending up in a rich man's tomb.
The second half insists on his innocence: "he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth." His burial among the wicked was undeserved.
Matthew 27:57–60
describes Joseph of Arimathea, "a rich man," placing Jesus in his own new tomb. Matthew does not cite
Isaiah 53:9
explicitly, so the connection rests on readers' recognition of the pattern.
1 Peter 2:22
does quote the verse's second half: "Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth."

runs.text: Isaiah 53:10
— "It pleased the LORD": offering, seed, and life

title.text: "It pleased the LORD": offering, seed, and life

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 53:10 — "It pleased the LORD": offering, seed, and life

runs.text: "Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand."
This verse is theologically sensitive and needs careful reading.

"It pleased the LORD to bruise him": the Hebrew verb means to will, intend, or purpose. It is the same root found later in the verse, "the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand." The repetition is deliberate. The servant's suffering was within God's purpose, and the same purpose will succeed through him. The verse does not say God enjoyed the servant's pain. It says the suffering was not meaningless or outside God's plan. Reading "pleased" as cruel satisfaction misreads both the Hebrew and the poem, which has spent several verses insisting that the servant suffered for others, not as an object of divine hostility.
"When thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin": the Hebrew word translated "offering for sin" is the term for the guilt offering, the sacrifice that made reparation for a wrong (
Leviticus 5
). The servant's life becomes the reparation that restores what was broken between God and the people.

The verse then turns. The one who was "cut off out of the land of the living" in verse 8 "shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days." This is language of life after death. The servant who died will see descendants and live long.
Mosiah 15:10–13

reads "his seed" as the faithful prophets and those who hearken to them. Christian readers have seen in this turn a pointer toward resurrection. In the poem itself, it is the beginning of divine vindication.

Many readers hear God's voice here, if it has not already resumed in verse 10b. "My righteous servant" supports that reading, although the text does not label its speakers.
"He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied": the servant will look on the result of his labor and be content. "Travail" in Hebrew means hard toil and trouble.

— A portion with the great, numbered with transgressors

title.text: A portion with the great, numbered with transgressors

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 53:12 — A portion with the great, numbered with transgressors

runs.text: "Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors."

The final verse uses the image of a victorious king sharing out the spoils of war. The servant receives a share with "the great" and divides spoil with "the strong." But the reason for his victory is the reverse of ordinary conquest. He has not taken lives. He has "poured out his soul unto death." He was "numbered with the transgressors," treated as a criminal. He "bare the sin of many" and "made intercession for the transgressors."
The servant's triumph comes through self-giving, not domination. He wins by losing his life. He pleads for the very people who wronged him.

runs.text: Christ in Isaiah 53
The textual case for reading Jesus in this chapter is the strongest anywhere in Isaiah:
Luke 22:37
records Jesus himself applying verse 12 to his arrest and death.
shows Philip preaching Jesus from verses 7–8.
Matthew 8:17
applies verse 4 to Jesus's healings.
John 12:38
and
Romans 10:16
apply verse 1 to unbelief in Jesus and the gospel.
uses verses 5, 6, and 9 to describe Christ's sinless suffering and its healing effect.
Abinadi quotes the full chapter and explains it as Christ's atonement (Mosiah 14–15).
develops the burden-bearing of verse 4 into an explanation of Christ's compassion.

These later uses do not erase the poem's ancient setting. The servant poem grew out of Israel's experience of exile, suffering among the nations, and hope for vindication. Jewish readers who see the servant as Israel are reading something real in the text. Christian readers believe Jesus took up this pattern and fulfilled it in a single, innocent life given for many. The poem's own movement, from misjudgment to confession, from suffering to vindication, prepared later readers to recognize him.

runs.text: Questions for study
Who might the "we" be in verses 1–6? How does the poem read differently depending on the answer?
Verse 4 reverses the speakers' assumption that the servant's suffering meant God had rejected him. What implications does this reversal have for how people interpret others' suffering?
Verse 5 combines medical, disciplinary, and legal images. What does each contribute that the others lack?
In verse 7 the servant is silent. What distinguishes his voluntary silence from the silence sometimes demanded of people being harmed? Why does that distinction matter?
How does "it pleased the LORD" in verse 10 read differently when connected with "the pleasure of the LORD" later in the same verse?
Verse 12 describes victory through self-giving and intercession. How does this differ from ordinary images of triumph?

runs.text: Chapter orientation

After the servant's suffering and vindication comes a song of joy for Zion. The barren mother bursts into singing, her tent expands, and God speaks to her as a husband restoring a wife he had sent away. The chapter returns to the marriage image of
and the barren mother of
and
. It answers both with abundance.
The placement is significant. Chapter 54 follows chapter 53 directly. The servant "shall see his seed" (
), and now Zion sees children she never expected.
In the Book of Mormon, the resurrected Jesus quotes the entire chapter in
3 Nephi 22
. A Scripture Central KnowHy reads this quotation as the covenant blessings that close Jesus's discourse on the covenant, applied to his Nephite audience (
Scripture Central, "Why Did Jesus Quote All of Isaiah 54?"

The marriage metaphor needs care. It describes God's relationship with a people, using an ancient image of marriage that differs from modern expectations. God's anger and hiddenness are metaphors for the exile's experience. They are never a model for how a husband should treat a wife. No one should use this chapter to justify enduring abuse or danger in a marriage.

Chapter orientation

The barren mother bursts into singing, her tent expands, and God speaks to her as a husband restoring a wife he had sent away. No one should use this chapter to justify enduring abuse or danger in a marriage.

runs.text: Isaiah 54:1
— Sing, barren one

title.text: Sing, barren one

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 54:1 — Sing, barren one

runs.text: "Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife, saith the LORD."
Zion is addressed as a barren woman. In ancient Israel, barrenness was deeply painful and often socially shameful (compare Hannah in
1 Samuel 1
). Now the barren woman is told to sing, because her children will outnumber those of the woman who was married all along.

The image is corporate. "The desolate" is the ruined city. The verse speaks of Jerusalem's repopulation by returning exiles, not of individual women's fertility. It does not promise biological children to anyone. It does not imply that childlessness reflects divine disfavor. If anything, it suggests that God's purposes are not limited to ordinary ways of building a family.
Paul quotes this verse in
Galatians 4:27

as part of an allegory contrasting the earthly Jerusalem with the "Jerusalem which is above," which "is free, which is the mother of us all." The barren woman's many children become all who belong to the covenant of promise through Christ, including Gentiles.

— Shame forgotten, Maker as husband

title.text: Shame forgotten, Maker as husband

runs.text: Verse 4

speaks to shame directly. "Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed: neither be thou confounded; for thou shalt not be put to shame: for thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth, and shalt not remember the reproach of thy widowhood any more." The word "shame" and its synonyms appear four times. "The shame of thy youth" may refer to Israel's early history, perhaps the Egyptian slavery or early unfaithfulness. "The reproach of thy widowhood" refers to the exile, when Zion was like a woman without a husband. Both will be forgotten. In the ancient Near East a widow often lost social protection, so "widowhood" here conveys vulnerability as well as grief.

— A small moment and an everlasting kindness

title.text: A small moment and an everlasting kindness

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 54:7–8 — A small moment and an everlasting kindness

runs.text: "For a small moment have I forsaken thee; but with great mercies will I gather thee. In a little wrath I hid my face from thee for a moment; but with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee, saith the LORD thy Redeemer."
These two verses are built on contrasts:
a "small moment" set against "great mercies";
"a little wrath" set against "everlasting kindness";
forsaking set against gathering;
hiding the face set against mercy.
In each pair, the second element vastly outweighs the first. The word translated "kindness" is a covenant term meaning steadfast, loyal love.
The verses must be read carefully. From God's perspective, the exile was "a small moment." For those who lived through it, it was decades, the loss of a temple, a homeland, and many lives.
Lamentations 5:20
asks, "Wherefore dost thou forget us for ever, and forsake us so long time?"
Isaiah 54:7–8
does not dismiss that lament. It does not say the suffering was small to those who suffered. It says that measured against God's everlasting kindness, even long pain is not the final word.
As a devotional application: these verses can offer perspective without demanding that anyone feel their own suffering is minor. The lament of Lamentations and the promise of

stand together in the canon.

headingRoot.text: Isaiah 55

runs.text: Chapter orientation

Chapter 55 is an invitation. After the servant's suffering (chapter 53) and Zion's restoration (chapter 54), God calls everyone who is thirsty to come and eat for free. The chapter is the conclusion of Isaiah 40–55. It ends where the section began, with the reliability of God's word (compare
and
The chapter moves in five stages:
a free feast (verses 1–2);
an everlasting covenant (verses 3–5);
a call to seek and return (verses 6–7);
God's higher ways (verses 8–9);
the effectiveness of God's word (verses 10–11), ending in a joyful exodus through singing creation (verses 12–13).
The lesson's emphasis on seeking the Lord is centered here.

— Free food, and food that fills

title.text: Free food, and food that fills

runs.text: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price." (
Verse 1

sounds like a market vendor calling to passersby. The invitation is paradoxical: "buy ... without money and without price." The water, wine, and milk are free. Water is basic survival. Wine and milk are luxury and nourishment. Everything needed is offered to everyone who is thirsty, especially "he that hath no money."
This is grace in its most concrete Old Testament form. Nothing is earned. Thirst is the only qualification.
Verse 2

asks why people spend money on what doesn't satisfy. "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness." The verse contrasts a costly pursuit that leaves people hungry with free abundance that satisfies. In the ancient world "fatness" meant rich food, the best of a feast.
The key move is "hearken diligently unto me." The way to eat is to listen. The food is God's word, God's covenant, God himself.

, where Jacob calls the poor to come and buy without money and not spend labor on what cannot satisfy. In
2 Nephi 26:25
, Nephi has the Lord invite all the ends of the earth to buy milk and honey without money and without price. In
John 7:37
, Jesus cries out at the feast, "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink."
Revelation 22:17
closes the Bible with the invitation to "whosoever will" to "take the water of life freely."

Verse 3: "Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David." Listening again leads to life. The "everlasting covenant" is described as "the sure mercies of David," meaning God's faithful covenant love promised to David.

runs.text: In
2 Samuel 7:12–16

God promised David a lasting dynasty. By the exile that dynasty seemed finished. The king was a prisoner in Babylon. Isaiah reapplies the promise to the whole people: what was promised to David is now extended to "you," plural. The Davidic covenant is democratized.
Paul, in
Acts 13:34

, quotes this verse in his argument that God raised Jesus from the dead: "I will give you the sure mercies of David." For Paul, the resurrection of Jesus, David's descendant, is how the sure mercies become permanent. A king who will never die again means a covenant that will never end.
Verse 4

: "Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people." "Him" is David, or the Davidic figure. He serves as witness and leader to the peoples. In Christian reading, the ultimate Davidic leader is Jesus (
Revelation 1:5
calls him "the faithful witness").
Verse 5

: "Behold, thou shalt call a nation that thou knowest not, and nations that knew not thee shall run unto thee because of the LORD thy God, and for the Holy One of Israel; for he hath glorified thee." The pronouns shift from "him" (David) in verse 4 to "thou" (Israel) in verse 5. The role David played toward the nations is now Israel's role. Nations Israel does not know will run to it, not because of Israel's power but because of the God who glorified it.
These pronoun shifts trace a pattern seen throughout this part of Isaiah. Roles move from an individual to the people and back. The servant becomes the servants (
). David's mercies become the people's covenant.

runs.text: Isaiah 55:6–7
— Seek, call, forsake, return

title.text: Seek, call, forsake, return

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 55:6–7 — Seek, call, forsake, return

runs.text: "Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near: Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon."
Verse 6

gives two parallel commands: "seek ye the LORD" and "call ye upon him." The time phrases, "while he may be found" and "while he is near," create urgency without suggesting God will hide. In context, God has come near in the announcement of redemption. Now is the time to respond.
Verse 7

spells out what seeking means. The wicked forsake their way. The unrighteous forsake their thoughts. Both actions and inner thinking are involved. Then comes the positive move: "let him return unto the LORD." "Return" in Hebrew is the main word for repentance, turning back.

The promise is generous: "he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon." "Abundantly" means multiplied, more than enough. Return does not meet a reluctant God. It meets mercy that overflows.
Doctrine and Covenants 88:62–63
echoes this invitation: "Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me."

runs.text: Isaiah 55:8–9
— Higher ways, in the context of mercy

title.text: Higher ways, in the context of mercy

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 55:8–9 — Higher ways, in the context of mercy

runs.text: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts."
These verses are often quoted on their own to explain why God's actions are beyond human understanding. That use is not entirely wrong. But the context changes their emphasis.

Verse 8 begins with "For," connecting it to verse 7. God's thoughts are higher than human thoughts in the specific matter just discussed: abundant pardon. Humans tend to forgive grudgingly and partially. God forgives abundantly. God's ways are higher in mercy.

Read this way, the verses are not primarily a conversation-stopper, a way to close down hard questions. They are an expansion of hope. Where human calculation would say a person has gone too far, God's thoughts reach higher.
This does not mean hard questions are forbidden. Isaiah itself is full of honest questions and complaints (
). Psalms of lament ask God directly why. The distance between God's thoughts and ours is a reason for humility and for hope, not a ban on sincere inquiry.

title.text: Rain, snow, and a word that does not come back empty

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 55:10–11 — Rain, snow, and a word that does not come back empty

runs.text: "For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."
Verse 10

describes the water cycle from an ancient observer's perspective. Rain and snow fall and don't go back up until they have watered the earth and made it fruitful. The verse ends with "seed to the sower, and bread to the eater," both future harvest and present food.
Verse 11

applies the image to God's word. Like rain, it goes out and does not return "void," empty. It accomplishes God's purpose and "prosper[s]" in its mission. The verb "prosper" also described the servant's success in
("the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand").
The section of Isaiah that began with "the word of our God shall stand for ever" (
) ends with that word's guaranteed effectiveness. The image connects with the food of verses 1–2. God's word is rain that produces bread. Listening is eating, and the word feeds.

The image also implies process. Rain does not produce bread overnight. There is planting, growing, and harvest. God's word works on its own timeline. Christian readers often connect this "word" with Christ, the Word made flesh (
John 1:14
), who was sent and accomplished his mission. That is a later theological connection, not the verse's explicit claim.

Chapter 56 begins a new section of Isaiah (chapters 56–66). The setting has shifted. The audience now seems to be the community back in the land, dealing with Sabbath, temple, and membership. The questions are practical: who belongs, and what does faithfulness look like in daily life?

The chapter has two contrasting halves. Verses 1–8 welcome foreigners and eunuchs who had feared exclusion. Verses 9–12 condemn leaders who neglect their responsibilities. Hilton's slides place this chapter under hope in the face of exclusion and link

). The discussion below reads those texts directly.

). That is an explicitly Latter-day Saint application alongside the ancient context of the Jerusalem sanctuary, not a replacement for it.

title.text: Justice and Sabbath as signs of nearness

runs.text: Verse 1

previewRoot.text:
Isaiah 56:1–2 — Justice and Sabbath as signs of nearness
Verse 1: "Thus saith the LORD, Keep ye judgment, and do justice: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed." The command is ethical: keep justice, do what is right. The motivation is the nearness of God's salvation.

runs.text: The word pair is significant. In earlier chapters "righteousness" and "salvation" described what God would do (

, 8). Now people are called to "do justice" (the same Hebrew root as "righteousness") because God's righteousness is about to be revealed. God's coming salvation is not a reason for passivity. It calls people to live in its light.
Verse 2

: "Blessed is the man that doeth this, and the son of man that layeth hold on it; that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and keepeth his hand from doing any evil." "Son of man" here means simply a human being. The blessing applies to anyone. Two practices are named together:
keeping the Sabbath;
keeping one's hand from evil.
Worship and ethics are inseparable. A person who keeps Sabbath while doing harm has missed the point. A person who avoids harm while neglecting worship has also missed something.
During and after the exile, Sabbath became an identity marker that could be kept anywhere, without a temple. Its prominence in this chapter reflects that.

runs.text: Isaiah 57

headingRoot.text: Isaiah 57

runs.text: Chapter orientation

Chapter 57 is the most difficult chapter in this week's reading. It begins with a lament for righteous people who die unnoticed. It then launches a fierce attack on idolatry, using sexual metaphors and describing child sacrifice. It closes with one of scripture's most tender passages, in which the high and holy God dwells with the contrite, heals, and speaks peace to the far and near.
The chapter's harsh imagery should be read as imagery in its context. The sexual language is a prophetic metaphor for covenant unfaithfulness, used throughout the prophets (
Hosea 2
Jeremiah 3
Ezekiel 16

). It is not a literal description of anyone's sexual conduct, and the text gives no basis for reconstructing specific rituals. The child sacrifice it describes was a real practice condemned elsewhere in scripture (
2 Kings 23:10
Jeremiah 7:31
). The chapter's condemnation of it is a defense of children, not permission for any cruelty.
The chapter ends with the refrain "There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked," which also closed
. This marks a section boundary.

runs.text: "The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart: and merciful men are taken away, none considering that the righteous is taken away from the evil to come." (
Verse 1
laments righteous and merciful people dying while no one pays attention. The community does not lay it to heart. In
the "we" failed to understand the servant's suffering. Here the community fails to notice the death of the righteous.

The final clause, "the righteous is taken away from the evil to come," suggests one possibility: the righteous may be spared coming trouble by dying before it arrives. This is offered as something the community fails to consider, not as an explanation of every righteous person's death. It should not be used to tell grieving people why their loved one died. Scripture does not claim that every death has a discernible reason, and this verse does not claim that either.
Verse 2

: "He shall enter into peace: they shall rest in their beds, each one walking in his uprightness." The righteous dead enter peace. "Rest in their beds" is a euphemism for the grave as a place of rest. "Each one walking in his uprightness" describes the lives they lived. The verse offers comfort without claiming to explain.
The contrast with the chapter's end is deliberate. The righteous "enter into peace" (verse 2). The wicked have "no peace" (verse 21).

). "Debase thyself even unto hell" uses "hell" for the Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead. The people have sunk as low as one can go.

: "Thou art wearied in the greatness of thy way; yet saidst thou not, There is no hope: thou hast found the life of thine hand; therefore thou wast not grieved." They found enough renewed strength, "the life of thine hand," to keep going, so they never stopped to grieve.

This verse has a psychological subtlety. Sometimes a person must reach the end of their own strength before they turn elsewhere. The people here kept finding just enough strength to continue their futile path. They never reached the point of admitting it wasn't working. Compare

title.text: The restless sea

previewRoot.text: Isaiah 57:20–21 — The restless sea

runs.text: "But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt. There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked."
Verse 20

uses the image of a storm-tossed sea that churns up mud. The "wicked" here are those who persist in the conduct the chapter has described: oppression, idolatry, child sacrifice, greed, refusal to turn. Their restlessness is the opposite of the righteous person's peace in verse 2.
Verse 21
completes the refrain: "There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked." The same words close
, marking the end of a section.

This contrast is covenantal and ethical. It describes the inner and outer turmoil that accompanies a life organized around harm and self-interest. It must not be used to diagnose anxiety, depression, or any mental illness as wickedness. Faithful people experience restlessness, distress, and psychological suffering, and people with clinical conditions are not the "wicked" of this verse. Scripture is full of righteous people in turmoil: Job, Jeremiah, the psalmists, and the servant of chapter 53. The servant was "a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief," and was not wicked.

The verse also follows directly after verse 19, which offered "Peace, peace to him that is far off." The far off include the wicked of verse 17, whom God has promised to heal. "No peace to the wicked" is not a permanent sentence. It describes the condition of those who refuse the peace God offers.

closingRoot.text:
Synthesis
These eight chapters move from a courtroom to a free feast, from a barren mother to a welcomed eunuch, from the servant's flint-set face to God dwelling with the crushed.
Several threads run through them:

The question of abandonment raised in 49:14 is answered from many angles. There is no final divorce decree (50:1). The servant is vindicated (52:13). Zion is restored in a covenant that will not be removed (54:10). The outsider receives an everlasting name (56:5).
The servant's experience becomes the pattern for the community. The servant listens, suffers, and is vindicated (50:4–9; 52:13–53:12). His followers become "servants" (54:17; 56:6) who share his vindication.
Suffering is never treated as proof of guilt. The speakers of 53:4 confess that they were wrong to assume the servant was "smitten of God." The righteous of 57:1 die without explanation, and the text laments rather than explains.
Grace and accountability stand together. Sin is named throughout, but God's last word is consistently healing, pardon, and comfort (55:7; 57:18–19).
The circle keeps widening. The barren woman's tent expands (54:2). Nations run to Israel (55:5). Foreigners and eunuchs are brought to the holy mountain (56:7). God gathers "others" beyond those already gathered (56:8).

Christian and Latter-day Saint readers find the center of these chapters in the servant of 52:13–53:12, whom the New Testament and the Book of Mormon identify as Jesus Christ. That identification rests on explicit later scripture, including Jesus's own words in Luke 22:37. It does not require erasing the poem's ancient setting or dismissing Jewish readings. It sees in one innocent life the fullest expression of a pattern Israel had long known: the one who bears others' griefs, is misjudged, dies, and is vindicated.
The chapters do not promise that faith prevents suffering. They promise that suffering does not have the last word, that the high and holy God is found with the crushed, and that a covenant of peace stands firmer than the mountains.

runs.text: A personal Latter-day Saint study resource for Come, Follow Me, October 12–18, 2026. This is not an official Church publication.
Introduction and Historical Context

Isaiah 58–66 closes one of scripture's most quoted books. The chapters begin by examining worship, especially fasting and the Sabbath, and end with new heavens and a new earth. Along the way the reader meets an anointed messenger, watchmen who will not stay silent, a warrior in red garments, a community praying through grief, and a mother city giving birth to a nation in a day. The reading is uneven by design. Accusation turns into promise, promise into lament, and lament into divine answer. Readers who expect a single smooth argument may feel lost. Readers who follow the changes of voice will find a conversation between a struggling people and a God who refuses to abandon them.
The setting the book gives
The book places Isaiah son of Amoz in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (
Isaiah 1:1
). This was Judah's eighth-century crisis under Assyrian pressure (see the
Bible Dictionary entry on Isaiah
). The final chapters, however, speak to a wider horizon:
Ruin.
The sanctuary has been "trodden down" (
). The "holy and beautiful house" has been "burned up with fire" (
Rebuilding.
Old wastes and "desolations of many generations" are to be rebuilt (
These images match the biblical record of Jerusalem's fall in
2 Kings 25
and the decree permitting return in
Ezra 1

. Scholars and believers have long discussed how these chapters relate to the eighth-century prophet. This guide does not try to settle questions of composition or set precise dates. It reads the chapters as they stand. They address a people living among ruins who are trying to worship faithfully, rebuild, and hope.
Three horizons of meaning
Several layers of meaning appear throughout this guide. They should be kept distinct:
The ancient horizon.
What the words said to Judah and Jerusalem, in poetry drawn from their landscape, temple, and history.
The Christian fulfillment.
Jesus read
Isaiah 61
in the Nazareth synagogue and declared it fulfilled (
). Paul quoted
Isaiah 59:20
and
Romans 11
Romans 10
The latter-day application.
The Restoration applies Zion, gathering, and the Second Coming to God's work now and in the future.

All three are legitimate, and none cancels the others. Jewish readers have treasured these chapters for millennia as promises to Israel and Jerusalem. A Christian reading does not need to dismiss that. Christ himself came to Zion as a son of Jacob.
What "Zion" means

In these chapters, Zion is first Jerusalem, often personified as a woman: bride, mother, or mourner. It is also God's gathered covenant community, defined by righteousness and his presence, which echoes the scriptural ideal of a people of "one heart and one mind" (
Moses 7:18

The images of nations bowing and bringing wealth (Isaiah 60–61) are poetic reversals of humiliation. They are not a charter for ethnic superiority or for dominating others today. Isaiah's own climax gathers "all nations and tongues" to see God's glory (
How the genres shift
Watch for these forms:
prophetic accusation (
communal confession (
the divine warrior (
salvation oracles and songs to Zion (60–62)
historical remembrance (
lament and prayer (63:15–64:12)
God's reply, with judgment and new creation (65–66)

"The Redeemer Shall Come to Zion"
, emphasizes several themes:
fasting that cares for the poor
the Sabbath as a delight
Jesus Christ as intercessor, healer, and Redeemer
Zion's light
Christ's future reign
It explicitly links
Isaiah 61
with

These are the threads I have chosen to follow. They are my own selection, made for close reading and personal application.

introductionRoot.text:
A personal Latter-day Saint study resource for Come, Follow Me, October 12–18, 2026. This is not an official Church publication.


Introduction and Historical Context
Isaiah 58–66 closes one of scripture's most quoted books. The chapters begin by examining worship, especially fasting and the Sabbath, and end with new heavens and a new earth. Along the way the reader meets an anointed messenger, watchmen who will not stay silent, a warrior in red garments, a community praying through grief, and a mother city giving birth to a nation in a day. The reading is uneven by design. Accusation turns into promise, promise into lament, and lament into divine answer. Readers who expect a single smooth argument may feel lost. Readers who follow the changes of voice will find a conversation between a struggling people and a God who refuses to abandon them.
The setting the book gives
The book places Isaiah son of Amoz in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1). This was Judah's eighth-century crisis under Assyrian pressure (see the Bible Dictionary entry on Isaiah). The final chapters, however, speak to a wider horizon:

Ruin. The sanctuary has been "trodden down" (63:18). The "holy and beautiful house" has been "burned up with fire" (64:10–11).
Rebuilding. Old wastes and "desolations of many generations" are to be rebuilt (58:12; 61:4).

These images match the biblical record of Jerusalem's fall in 2 Kings 25 and the decree permitting return in Ezra 1. Scholars and believers have long discussed how these chapters relate to the eighth-century prophet. This guide does not try to settle questions of composition or set precise dates. It reads the chapters as they stand. They address a people living among ruins who are trying to worship faithfully, rebuild, and hope.
Three horizons of meaning
Several layers of meaning appear throughout this guide. They should be kept distinct:

The ancient horizon. What the words said to Judah and Jerusalem, in poetry drawn from their landscape, temple, and history.
The Christian fulfillment. Jesus read Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue and declared it fulfilled (Luke 4:16–21). Paul quoted Isaiah 59:20 and 65:1–2 (Romans 11; Romans 10).
The latter-day application. The Restoration applies Zion, gathering, and the Second Coming to God's work now and in the future.

All three are legitimate, and none cancels the others. Jewish readers have treasured these chapters for millennia as promises to Israel and Jerusalem. A Christian reading does not need to dismiss that. Christ himself came to Zion as a son of Jacob.
What "Zion" means
In these chapters, Zion is first Jerusalem, often personified as a woman: bride, mother, or mourner. It is also God's gathered covenant community, defined by righteousness and his presence, which echoes the scriptural ideal of a people of "one heart and one mind" (Moses 7:18).
The images of nations bowing and bringing wealth (Isaiah 60–61) are poetic reversals of humiliation. They are not a charter for ethnic superiority or for dominating others today. Isaiah's own climax gathers "all nations and tongues" to see God's glory (66:18).
How the genres shift
Watch for these forms:

prophetic accusation (58:1–5; 59:1–8)
communal confession (59:9–15)
the divine warrior (59:15–20; 63:1–6)
salvation oracles and songs to Zion (60–62)
historical remembrance (63:7–14)
lament and prayer (63:15–64:12)
God's reply, with judgment and new creation (65–66)

The official lesson in brief
The Church's lesson for this week, "The Redeemer Shall Come to Zion", emphasizes several themes:

fasting that cares for the poor
the Sabbath as a delight
Jesus Christ as intercessor, healer, and Redeemer
Zion's light
Christ's future reign

It explicitly links Isaiah 61 with Luke 4:16–21, and it points readers to President Henry B. Eyring's 2015 message on fasting.


Significant Points for This Week
These are the threads I have chosen to follow. They are my own selection, made for close reading and personal application.

True worship includes our neighbor. Isaiah 58 does not reject fasting or the Sabbath. It refuses to let them become private performances while workers are exploited and the hungry go unfed.
God's arm acts when no one else can. "There was no man… no intercessor" (59:16; compare 63:5). The Redeemer intervenes in a world where human justice has collapsed.
Light is received before it is reflected. "Arise, shine; for thy light is come" (60:1). Zion shines because the Lord rises on her, not because of her own brilliance.
The Anointed One exchanges ashes for beauty. Isaiah 61 is the mission statement Jesus claimed for himself. It is about binding, freeing, comforting, and clothing.
New names mark renewed covenant. Forsaken becomes Hephzibah, and Desolate becomes Beulah (62:4).
Judgment and mercy both belong to redemption. The red-garmented warrior of 63:1–6 is first a figure of judgment. The chapter then pivots to God's tender suffering with his people (63:9).
Honest lament is a form of faith. Isaiah 63:15–64:12 models praying through disaster with confession, protest, and trust: "we are the clay, and thou our potter."
God answers with a new creation. Isaiah 65–66 describe secure homes, long lives, answered prayers, and worship by "all flesh." The book still ends soberly, warning that rebellion has consequences.
