runs.text: Isaiah 58:1–2
— A Trumpet Against Religious People

title.text: A Trumpet Against Religious People

runs.text: The prophet is told to cry "like a trumpet," the instrument that sounded alarms and assembled people for holy days. The target is surprising. The people are not careless pagans. They "seek me daily," "delight to know my ways," and "take delight in approaching to God."

previewRoot.text:
Isaiah 58:1–2 — A Trumpet Against Religious People
The prophet is told to cry "like a trumpet," the instrument that sounded alarms and assembled people for holy days. The target is surprising. The people are not careless pagans. They "seek me daily," "delight to know my ways," and "take delight in approaching to God."

runs.text: Verse 2 says they behave "as a nation that did righteousness." The word "as" carries the critique: the outward form resembles covenant faithfulness. The irony is gentle but sharp. Their religious activity is visible, but the comparison exposes a gap between ritual and righteousness. They want God's "ordinances of justice," meaning his rulings and decisions, while ignoring justice toward others.
Application:
Regular religious activity can coexist with blind spots. The chapter tests the people's seeking by asking what it has produced in their treatment of others.

— Complaints at the Fast and God's Reply

title.text: Complaints at the Fast and God's Reply

runs.text: The people's complaint (verse 3a).
Isaiah quotes the people's own words: "Wherefore have we fasted… and thou seest not?" Fasting has become a transaction. We afflict ourselves, so God should notice.

previewRoot.text:
Isaiah 58:3–5 — Complaints at the Fast and God's Reply
The people's complaint (verse 3a). Isaiah quotes the people's own words: "Wherefore have we fasted… and thou seest not?" Fasting has become a transaction. We afflict ourselves, so God should notice.

runs.text: God's answer (verses 3b–4).
"In the day of your fast ye find pleasure, and exact all your labours." Employers fast while still driving their workers.
The fast produces "strife and debate" and even violence, "the fist of wickedness."
Such fasting will not "make your voice to be heard on high."
The rhetorical questions (verse 5).

These questions mock fasting reduced to display: bowing the head "as a bulrush," a reed drooping in the wind, and lying on "sackcloth and ashes." These were genuine mourning customs. God is not condemning them. He is asking whether posture alone can be "an acceptable day to the Lord."

— Loosing Bands and Opening the House

title.text: Loosing Bands and Opening the House

runs.text: God now defines the fast he has "chosen." The verbs pile up:
loose, undo, let go free, break

previewRoot.text:
Isaiah 58:6–7 — Loosing Bands and Opening the House
God now defines the fast he has "chosen." The verbs pile up: loose, undo, let go free, break every yoke. Then come concrete acts:

runs.text: dealing bread to the hungry
bringing the "poor that are cast out" into one's house
covering the naked
refusing to "hide… from thine own flesh"
That last phrase treats the needy as kin. Avoiding them is a form of hiding.
This is the core of the chapter. Fasting does not become less spiritual. It becomes more embodied. The hunger of the faster is joined to the hunger of the neighbor. Compare
Matthew 25:35–40
, where feeding and clothing "the least of these" is service to Christ himself.
Official teaching:
President Henry B. Eyring taught that fast offerings both relieve physical need and change the giver's heart, and he connected succoring others with serving Christ in
Matthew 25
Eyring, 2015

Elder Ulisses Soares, in October 2026, described a fast that joins joyful worship, purposeful prayer, trust in God's will, and generous care for others. He taught that generous fast offerings put Isaiah's lifting of burdens into practice. He also observed that fasting and prayer may give strength to carry a burden rather than remove it, and that answers may differ from what we expect (
Soares, "A Higher and Holier Fast"
). His footnote recognizes those whose health does not allow fasting, nursing mothers, and young children who should not be compelled. Isaiah's emphasis on relieving burdens fits that compassion.
Teaching suggestion:
Jonn Claybaugh's 2022 Interpreter Foundation study aid invites readers to list the acts named in
Isaiah 58:6–7
, then choose one and plan a specific way to improve in living the fast (
study aid
). It is an independent study aid, not official Church teaching, but it turns the chapter's many verbs into a single achievable step.

runs.text: Isaiah 60:1–3
— Light Has Come

title.text: Light Has Come

runs.text: "Arise, shine; for thy light is come." The commands are addressed to Zion as a woman, perhaps lying in the dust of mourning. The reason precedes her action: light has already come, and "the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee."

previewRoot.text:
Isaiah 60:1–3 — Light Has Come
"Arise, shine; for thy light is come." The commands are addressed to Zion as a woman, perhaps lying in the dust of mourning. The reason precedes her action: light has already come, and "the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee."

runs.text: Verse 2 sets the contrast: "darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people," but the Lord "shall arise upon thee." Zion's glory is reflected glory, like a city catching the dawn.
Verse 3: "the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising." Zion does not conquer the nations. She attracts them.
Christ connection:
Jesus is "the light of the world" and tells his followers to let their light shine (
John 8:12
Matthew 5:14–16
). The order is the same: received light, then shared light.

Study Plan and Teaching Discussion
A seven-day personal plan

Day 1: Isaiah 58. Read verses 3–7 aloud. Plan a fast with a specific purpose. Consider whether a fast offering could be more generous. If health does not permit fasting, choose another act of burden-lifting.
Day 2: Isaiah 59. Mark every body part named in verses 3–8. Then read verses 16–21 and write what "intercessor" means to you.
Day 3: Isaiah 60. Underline every reference to light. Ask where you have received light that you could now reflect.
Day 4: Isaiah 61–62. Read Luke 4:16–21 next to Isaiah 61:1–3. List the three exchanges and the new names, and choose one that speaks to you.
Day 5: Isaiah 63. Read verses 1–6 first as a judgment scene. Then read Doctrine and Covenants 19:16–19 and verses 7–9. Reflect on how the same Lord brings justice and suffers with his people.
Day 6: Isaiah 64. Write your own short lament in the pattern of 63:15–64:12: remembrance, honest confession, "Thou art our father," and a plea.
Day 7: Isaiah 65–66. Read God's answer. Compare 65:24 with 64:7, and 66:23 with 58:13. Notice how the book closes the circle.

Teaching ideas for home or class

Two kinds of fast. Divide the board into "the fast they chose" (58:3–5) and "the fast God chose" (58:6–10), and let learners fill in each column from the text.
Name changes. List the old and new names in 60:14, 18; 61:3, 6; and 62:2, 4, 12. Ask: what is God saying about identity?
Justice and mercy. Teach Isaiah 63 in two steps. Start with the plain text of judgment, then the devotional connection to the Atonement. Ask how both comfort the oppressed.
Lament as faith. Ask whether it is acceptable to say to God what 63:17 or 64:12 says. Discuss how confession and protest coexist in faithful prayer.
Ordinary blessings. Use 65:21–23 to discuss homes, work, and children as places of salvation. Be sensitive to learners who experience childlessness or insecure housing. Isaiah's promise is God's future, not a measure of anyone's present righteousness.

Discussion questions spanning the chapters

How do Isaiah 58's fast and Isaiah 66's universal Sabbath frame the whole section?
The divine "arm" appears in 59:16, 62:8, and 63:5, 12. What does it mean that God's own arm saves?
How does Jesus's reading of Isaiah 61 shape the way we read the rest of these chapters?
Where in these chapters do you see God answering a specific complaint or prayer from earlier in the reading?

This is a personal Latter-day Saint study guide, not an official publication of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. It follows the week's assignment in the
official 2026 Come, Follow Me lesson

and quotes scripture from the King James Version. Throughout, I try to separate four kinds of statements: what a passage most likely meant in Jeremiah's world, what Latter-day Saints officially teach from it, what particular scholars have proposed, and my own devotional application. Those categories often support one another, but they are not the same thing.
Historical and Literary Context
Jeremiah was "the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin" (
Jeremiah 1:1

). Anathoth was a village a few miles northeast of Jerusalem. Hilkiah was a common name. Some readers identify Jeremiah's father with the high priest Hilkiah who found the book of the law in Josiah's temple (
2 Kings 22:8
), but the text never makes that connection, and the phrase "priests that were in Anathoth" more naturally suggests a village priestly family.
The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah "in the thirteenth year" of King Josiah (

), about 627/626 BC. Josiah's reign brought a sweeping reform: local shrines were torn down and worship was centralized in Jerusalem (2 Kings 22–23). Josiah died at Megiddo, his son Jehoahaz reigned only briefly, and Pharaoh then placed Jehoiakim on the throne (
). Babylon soon became the dominant power. Under Jehoiachin, the city's treasures and many of its leaders were carried to Babylon (
). Zedekiah reigned until Jerusalem and its temple were destroyed about 587/586 BC. (
Jeremiah 52:12–13
.) Jeremiah lived through all of it, and later chapters show him carried to Egypt by survivors (
Jeremiah 43:6–7
). The
Bible Dictionary
reports a tradition that he was stoned there; it is a tradition, not a biblical record. We do not know his age at his call or the circumstances of his death.
Latter-day Saints remember that Jeremiah was Lehi's contemporary.
Jonn Claybaugh's study aid
gathers the Book of Mormon references: Jeremiah's prophecies were on the brass plates (
1 Nephi 5:13
), Nephi's brothers knew he had been imprisoned (
1 Nephi 7:14
), and Nephi the son of Helaman later cited him (
Helaman 8:20
The book of Jeremiah is not a diary arranged in order. It is a set of collections: poetic oracles, prose sermons, biographical stories, and personal laments.
Jeremiah 36
describes how the prophet dictated his words to Baruch, how the king burned the scroll, and how it was rewritten "and there were added besides unto them many like words" (

). The Bible Dictionary groups chapters 1–6 under Josiah and 7–20 under Jehoiakim. That grouping is a helpful approximation, but many individual oracles in this week's chapters cannot be dated precisely.
Three features of the writing need care:
Several voices.
God speaks, Jeremiah speaks, a narrator speaks, and sometimes the people speak, quoted or imagined. Noticing who is talking prevents us from treating a prophet's anguished prayer as a divine command.

Chapters 2–3 picture the covenant as a marriage between the Lord and Israel and describe idolatry as adultery. The "wife" is the whole nation: kings, priests, and the men who ran its courts and shrines. The metaphor indicts covenant betrayal. It does not rank women as morally lower, justify violence, or model how human spouses should treat each other.

John 9:2–3

). Custom and the calendar vary, so not every community reads these passages the same way every year. Christians and Latter-day Saints reading Jeremiah are reading the inheritance of a living people, not just an archive of ancient Israel's failures.
Significant Insights for This Week
John Hilton III's class slides

for this lesson organize the week around one question: how does God's word come to live deep in a person's heart, as it burned in Jeremiah's? The slides follow that question through four movements: being called, rejecting counterfeit devotion, choosing to turn back, and yielding to the potter. The question is worth keeping in mind through every chapter. Here are six threads I found especially illuminating.
1. The God who forms.
In
Jeremiah 1:5
, "Before I formed thee" uses the Hebrew verb
yatsar
, the potter's word. The same root names the potter in
Jeremiah 18:2–6
and describes God "framing" disaster in
. It is also the verb of
Genesis 2:7
, where the Lord "formed man of the dust" (see the public-domain lexical entry,
Strong's 3335
). The lesson's title verse and its potter chapter share the vocabulary of shaping. Jeremiah was formed for a calling, and a nation was still on the wheel.
2. The grammar of returning.
Hilton's slides note how Jeremiah plays on the Hebrew root
shuv
("turn, return"): "backsliding" (
meshubah
) and "return" come from the same word.
Jeremiah 3:22

compresses the whole gospel of repentance into that wordplay: "Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings." People who have turned away can turn again, and God heals the turning itself.
3. Fountain or cistern.
Water runs through these chapters: the "fountain of living waters" and leaking cisterns (
), the Nile and Euphrates of foreign alliances (
), the tree planted by the waters (
), the Lord named again as the fountain (
), and the snow and cold streams of Lebanon (
). The underlying question is always where a people draws its life.
4. Holy places require holy lives.
Jeremiah preaches at the temple gate (
), foresees a day without the ark (
), and stands at the city gates about the Sabbath (

). He does not despise any of these. He refuses to let them stand in for justice and loyalty. The Bible Dictionary identifies inwardness as one of the prophet's central themes: outward service is useless without devotion of heart and life.
5. The womb at both ends.
The lesson title celebrates 1:5: "before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee." The week's last verse asks: "Wherefore came I forth out of the womb to see labour and sorrow?" (
). The same image frames a sacred call and a devastating lament. Being known by God before birth did not make Jeremiah's life easy, and scripture keeps both verses.
6. Judgment is not the last word.
Some of the bleakest chapters in scripture contain gathering promises: one of a city and two of a family brought to Zion (
), and a new exodus that will outshine the old (
). Ancient readers saw return from exile. Latter-day Saints also see an ongoing latter-day gathering. In these chapters, the same God who announces scattering also promises to bring His people home.

1. The God who forms. In Jeremiah 1:5, "Before I formed thee" uses the Hebrew verb yatsar, the potter's word. The same root names the potter in Jeremiah 18:2–6 and describes God "framing" disaster in 18:11. It is also the verb of Genesis 2:7, where the Lord "formed man of the dust" (see the public-domain lexical entry, Strong's 3335). The lesson's title verse and its potter chapter share the vocabulary of shaping. Jeremiah was formed for a calling, and a nation was still on the wheel.
2. The grammar of returning. Hilton's slides note how Jeremiah plays on the Hebrew root shuv ("turn, return"): "backsliding" (meshubah) and "return" come from the same word. Jeremiah 3:22 compresses the whole gospel of repentance into that wordplay: "Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings." People who have turned away can turn again, and God heals the turning itself.
3. Fountain or cistern. Water runs through these chapters: the "fountain of living waters" and leaking cisterns (2:13), the Nile and Euphrates of foreign alliances (2:18), the tree planted by the waters (17:8), the Lord named again as the fountain (17:13), and the snow and cold streams of Lebanon (18:14). The underlying question is always where a people draws its life.
4. Holy places require holy lives. Jeremiah preaches at the temple gate (7:2), foresees a day without the ark (3:16), and stands at the city gates about the Sabbath (17:19). He does not despise any of these. He refuses to let them stand in for justice and loyalty. The Bible Dictionary identifies inwardness as one of the prophet's central themes: outward service is useless without devotion of heart and life.
5. The womb at both ends. The lesson title celebrates 1:5: "before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee." The week's last verse asks: "Wherefore came I forth out of the womb to see labour and sorrow?" (20:18). The same image frames a sacred call and a devastating lament. Being known by God before birth did not make Jeremiah's life easy, and scripture keeps both verses.
6. Judgment is not the last word. Some of the bleakest chapters in scripture contain gathering promises: one of a city and two of a family brought to Zion (3:14), and a new exodus that will outshine the old (16:14–15). Ancient readers saw return from exile. Latter-day Saints also see an ongoing latter-day gathering. In these chapters, the same God who announces scattering also promises to bring His people home.

runs.text: Jeremiah 17:11
— The Partridge Proverb

title.text: The Partridge Proverb

runs.text: "As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool." This is a proverb, built on an ancient folk observation about a bird whose brooding comes to nothing. The point is not ornithology. It is the emptiness of wealth gained unjustly, which deserts its owner. Jesus told of a rich man God called "fool" on the night his life was required (
Luke 12:20
). The verse condemns exploiters; it is not a claim that the exploited lose their reward.

runs.text: Come, Follow Me study week:
October 26–November 1, 2026
Readings:
Jeremiah 31–33; 36–39;
Lamentations 1

This is a personal Latter-day Saint study guide. It is not an official publication of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. It works through every verse in this week's reading: 40 verses of
Jeremiah 31
, 44 of
Jeremiah 32
, 26 of
Jeremiah 33
, 32 of
Jeremiah 36
, 21 of
Jeremiah 37
, 28 of
Jeremiah 38
, 18 of
Jeremiah 39
, 22 of
Lamentations 1
, and 66 of
Lamentations 3

Bible quotations come from the King James Version. Most of the discussion is my own close reading of those chapters. Where a modern resource has shaped a point, the guide names it briefly in the text, and all of these resources are listed at the end.
The guide also tries to keep four kinds of statements separate:
Ancient context:
what the text likely meant in Jeremiah's world.
Official Church teaching:
what Church publications teach.
Scholars' proposals:
individual interpretations, which remain open to discussion.
Application:
devotional uses for our own lives.
These chapters hold some of the most hopeful promises in the Old Testament. They also hold some of its darkest scenes. The week's title comes from
Jeremiah 31:13
. In these chapters, joy does not erase mourning. The promise is that the Lord will turn mourning into joy, and that turning happens with grief still in view.
Historical and Literary Context
A book arranged by collections.
Jeremiah is not a diary told in order. It gathers oracles, poems, prayers, and stories into collections, so the reader moves back and forth in time.
Chapters 30–31
are poetry of restoration and are often called a book of consolation.
Chapters 32–33
take place during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. Chapter 32 is dated to the tenth year of King Zedekiah. Chapter 33 continues while Jeremiah is still confined and gives no new date.
Chapter 36
jumps back to the fourth and fifth years of King Jehoiakim, about 605/604 BC.
Chapters 37–39
return to the final siege and the fall of the city.
Approximate dates.
Dates for this period are approximate, and scholars often differ by a year.
Jeremiah's call
came in Josiah's thirteenth year, about 627/626 BC (
Jeremiah 1:2
His ministry
continued past Jerusalem's fall and ended in Egypt (
Jeremiah 43–44
). The Bible does not record when or how he died.
Josiah
died about 609 BC.
Jehoahaz
ruled briefly after him.
Jehoiakim
reigned about 609–598.
Jehoiachin
(also called Coniah or Jeconiah) reigned about three months before being taken to Babylon in 597.
Zedekiah
reigned from 597 until Jerusalem fell, about 587/586.
The final siege.
Babylon's siege began in Zedekiah's ninth year, in the tenth month (
Jeremiah 39:1
A brief reprieve.
An Egyptian army caused a short break in the siege (
Jeremiah 37:5
Jeremiah 32–33.
Chapter 32 is dated to Zedekiah's tenth year, around 588/587. Chapter 33 follows while Jeremiah is still shut up in the court of the prison (
Jeremiah 33:1
) and supplies no new date.
The breach.
The wall was broken in Zedekiah's eleventh year, fourth month.
The temple burned
a month later, in the fifth month (
Jeremiah 52:12–13
). These are two separate events and should not be merged.
The Book of Mormon begins in this same world: Lehi preached "in the commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah" (
1 Nephi 1:4
Lamentations.
Lamentations is five poems of grief written after Jerusalem fell.
Authorship.
The book itself names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition credit Jeremiah, and the Church's
Guide to the Scriptures
presents it as his work, written after the fall around 586 BC. Because the text is anonymous, this guide treats Jeremiah's authorship as traditional and respected but not certain.
Acrostics.
Chapter 1 has 22 verses, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
Chapter 3
expands the pattern to 66 verses, with three verses in a row for each letter.
The alphabet form is itself meaningful. Grief is given order, from first letter to last, without pretending the grief is small.
Reading judgment and lament responsibly.
Jeremiah and Lamentations interpret the fall of Jerusalem as a national covenant crisis.
Not a diagnosis.
These texts are not a tool for deciding why a particular person today is suffering. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning (
John 9:2–3
Luke 13:1–5
Not a verdict on Jewish people.
Lamentations confesses sin in Zion's own voice. That confession never gives outsiders permission to call Jewish suffering, ancient or modern, deserved.
The promises still stand.
The covenant promises to Israel and Judah here are real and lasting. The Book of Mormon rebukes Gentiles who forget the Jews, whom the Lord calls "mine ancient covenant people" (
2 Nephi 29:4–5
Christ connections are labeled.

Christian readings, and Latter-day Saint readings in particular, find Christ in this material. This guide marks when a connection is explicit in later scripture, when it is official interpretation, and when it is typology or devotional application.
Significant Insights
1. The prophet who uprooted was also called to plant.
Jeremiah's call had six verbs: "to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant" (
Jeremiah 1:10
). The
official 2026 lesson
uses that verse to ask how a life left in ruins by sin or hardship can be rebuilt.
Jeremiah 31:28
answers with the same vocabulary. God, who watched over Judah to pluck up and break down, will watch over them "to build, and to plant."
Jeremiah 32
then acts it out: a real field is bought in a land about to be lost.
2. Hope can be signed, sealed, witnessed, and buried in a jar.
Jeremiah 32

does not show hope as a mood. It shows a legal act: silver weighed, a deed signed and sealed, witnesses gathered, and copies stored for a long future. Faith in God's promises can take concrete, careful, public form even when the outward evidence points the other way.
3. Covenant loyalty runs through the week.
Avram R. Shannon's short
Scripture Central entry on
ḥesed

explains that this Hebrew word is hard to translate. At its core it means covenant loyalty, the faithful conduct proper to a covenant relationship. The KJV often renders it "mercy" or "lovingkindness" because that is how the Lord treats His covenant people. Shannon also notes that the Lord wants the same loyalty from His people, not just general niceness.
His list of related passages includes four verses in this week's reading:
Jeremiah 31:3
Jeremiah 32:18
Jeremiah 33:11
Lamentations 3:22
Read side by side, those verses show God's steady covenant love running underneath both judgment and restoration.
4. God's word outlasts the fire.
John Hilton III's
class slides
organize this material around a question: what do people do when God's word is hard to accept? His slides answer partly through
Jeremiah 36
. A king cuts and burns the scroll, and the Lord simply has it written again, with more added.
Jehoiakim rejects the word with a knife. Zedekiah keeps asking for the word but will not obey it. Both are warnings, and both are mirrors.
5. Courage often comes from the margins.

The man who saves Jeremiah from the cistern is not a priest or a prince. He is Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian court official whose name means "servant of the king." He uses the access he has, says plainly that something is wrong, and handles the rescue with practical gentleness. The Lord later tells him that He knows he was afraid (
Jeremiah 39:17
6. Lament is faithful speech.
Scripture Helps
points out that Lamentations, unlike many Old Testament books, records no response from the Lord. It holds the people's grief and longing as they are.
That is a gift. Scripture gives sufferers words for what they feel and does not force a quick resolution. Even the famous hope of
Lamentations 3:21–24
rises from inside remembered pain, and the chapter ends with a cry for justice rather than calm.
7. The promises to Israel and Judah endure.
Jeremiah 31:35–37

and 33:19–26 tie Israel's continued existence to sunrise, moonlight, and the tides. Christians, including Latter-day Saints, read the new covenant through Jesus Christ. Reading it well means rejoicing in that fulfillment without claiming that God has cast off the people He named in these very verses.

Bible quotations come from the King James Version. Most of the discussion is my own close reading of those chapters. Where a modern resource has shaped a point, the guide names it briefly in the text, and all of these resources are listed at the end.
The guide also tries to keep four kinds of statements separate:

Ancient context: what the text likely meant in Jeremiah's world.
Official Church teaching: what Church publications teach.
Scholars' proposals: individual interpretations, which remain open to discussion.
Application: devotional uses for our own lives.

These chapters hold some of the most hopeful promises in the Old Testament. They also hold some of its darkest scenes. The week's title comes from Jeremiah 31:13. In these chapters, joy does not erase mourning. The promise is that the Lord will turn mourning into joy, and that turning happens with grief still in view.


Historical and Literary Context
A book arranged by collections. Jeremiah is not a diary told in order. It gathers oracles, poems, prayers, and stories into collections, so the reader moves back and forth in time.

Chapters 30–31 are poetry of restoration and are often called a book of consolation.
Chapters 32–33 take place during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem. Chapter 32 is dated to the tenth year of King Zedekiah. Chapter 33 continues while Jeremiah is still confined and gives no new date.
Chapter 36 jumps back to the fourth and fifth years of King Jehoiakim, about 605/604 BC.
Chapters 37–39 return to the final siege and the fall of the city.

Approximate dates. Dates for this period are approximate, and scholars often differ by a year.

Jeremiah's call came in Josiah's thirteenth year, about 627/626 BC (Jeremiah 1:2).
His ministry continued past Jerusalem's fall and ended in Egypt (Jeremiah 43–44). The Bible does not record when or how he died.
Josiah died about 609 BC.
Jehoahaz ruled briefly after him.
Jehoiakim reigned about 609–598.
Jehoiachin (also called Coniah or Jeconiah) reigned about three months before being taken to Babylon in 597.
Zedekiah reigned from 597 until Jerusalem fell, about 587/586.

The final siege. Babylon's siege began in Zedekiah's ninth year, in the tenth month (Jeremiah 39:1).

A brief reprieve. An Egyptian army caused a short break in the siege (Jeremiah 37:5).
Jeremiah 32–33. Chapter 32 is dated to Zedekiah's tenth year, around 588/587. Chapter 33 follows while Jeremiah is still shut up in the court of the prison (Jeremiah 33:1) and supplies no new date.
The breach. The wall was broken in Zedekiah's eleventh year, fourth month.
The temple burned a month later, in the fifth month (Jeremiah 52:12–13). These are two separate events and should not be merged.

The Book of Mormon begins in this same world: Lehi preached "in the commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah" (1 Nephi 1:4).
Lamentations. Lamentations is five poems of grief written after Jerusalem fell.

Authorship. The book itself names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition credit Jeremiah, and the Church's Guide to the Scriptures presents it as his work, written after the fall around 586 BC. Because the text is anonymous, this guide treats Jeremiah's authorship as traditional and respected but not certain.
Acrostics. Chapter 1 has 22 verses, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
Chapter 3 expands the pattern to 66 verses, with three verses in a row for each letter.

The alphabet form is itself meaningful. Grief is given order, from first letter to last, without pretending the grief is small.
Reading judgment and lament responsibly. Jeremiah and Lamentations interpret the fall of Jerusalem as a national covenant crisis.

Not a diagnosis. These texts are not a tool for deciding why a particular person today is suffering. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning (John 9:2–3; Luke 13:1–5).
Not a verdict on Jewish people. Lamentations confesses sin in Zion's own voice. That confession never gives outsiders permission to call Jewish suffering, ancient or modern, deserved.
The promises still stand. The covenant promises to Israel and Judah here are real and lasting. The Book of Mormon rebukes Gentiles who forget the Jews, whom the Lord calls "mine ancient covenant people" (2 Nephi 29:4–5).
Christ connections are labeled. Christian readings, and Latter-day Saint readings in particular, find Christ in this material. This guide marks when a connection is explicit in later scripture, when it is official interpretation, and when it is typology or devotional application.



Significant Insights
1. The prophet who uprooted was also called to plant. Jeremiah's call had six verbs: "to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant" (Jeremiah 1:10). The official 2026 lesson uses that verse to ask how a life left in ruins by sin or hardship can be rebuilt.
Jeremiah 31:28 answers with the same vocabulary. God, who watched over Judah to pluck up and break down, will watch over them "to build, and to plant." Jeremiah 32 then acts it out: a real field is bought in a land about to be lost.
2. Hope can be signed, sealed, witnessed, and buried in a jar. Jeremiah 32 does not show hope as a mood. It shows a legal act: silver weighed, a deed signed and sealed, witnesses gathered, and copies stored for a long future. Faith in God's promises can take concrete, careful, public form even when the outward evidence points the other way.
3. Covenant loyalty runs through the week. Avram R. Shannon's short Scripture Central entry on ḥesed explains that this Hebrew word is hard to translate. At its core it means covenant loyalty, the faithful conduct proper to a covenant relationship. The KJV often renders it "mercy" or "lovingkindness" because that is how the Lord treats His covenant people. Shannon also notes that the Lord wants the same loyalty from His people, not just general niceness.
His list of related passages includes four verses in this week's reading:

Jeremiah 31:3
Jeremiah 32:18
Jeremiah 33:11
Lamentations 3:22

Read side by side, those verses show God's steady covenant love running underneath both judgment and restoration.
4. God's word outlasts the fire. John Hilton III's class slides organize this material around a question: what do people do when God's word is hard to accept? His slides answer partly through Jeremiah 36. A king cuts and burns the scroll, and the Lord simply has it written again, with more added.
Jehoiakim rejects the word with a knife. Zedekiah keeps asking for the word but will not obey it. Both are warnings, and both are mirrors.
5. Courage often comes from the margins. The man who saves Jeremiah from the cistern is not a priest or a prince. He is Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian court official whose name means "servant of the king." He uses the access he has, says plainly that something is wrong, and handles the rescue with practical gentleness. The Lord later tells him that He knows he was afraid (Jeremiah 39:17).
6. Lament is faithful speech. Scripture Helps points out that Lamentations, unlike many Old Testament books, records no response from the Lord. It holds the people's grief and longing as they are.
That is a gift. Scripture gives sufferers words for what they feel and does not force a quick resolution. Even the famous hope of Lamentations 3:21–24 rises from inside remembered pain, and the chapter ends with a cry for justice rather than calm.
7. The promises to Israel and Judah endure. Jeremiah 31:35–37 and 33:19–26 tie Israel's continued existence to sunrise, moonlight, and the tides. Christians, including Latter-day Saints, read the new covenant through Jesus Christ. Reading it well means rejoicing in that fulfillment without claiming that God has cast off the people He named in these very verses.

runs.text: Verse 22 asks, "How long wilt thou go about, O thou backsliding daughter?" picturing someone wandering and hesitating. Then it gives a reason to come back: "the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man."
This line is one of the hardest in Jeremiah. Interpreters have proposed several meanings:
A reversal of roles, where Israel (pictured as a woman) seeks out or embraces her divine husband.
A proverb for something unheard of.
A messianic reading, proposed by some later Christian interpreters.
The context does not settle the question, and confident claims are best avoided. What is clear is that the "new thing" is God's work, and it is meant to end Israel's wandering.

What "waymarks" — memories, people, covenants — help you find the road back?

The Lord introduces Himself as Creator: the One "which giveth the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, which divideth the sea when the waves thereof roar." The word "ordinances" here means the fixed decrees of nature.

runs.text: Verse 36 builds an argument from them: if those decrees ever fail, "then the seed of Israel also shall cease from being a nation before me for ever." Verse 37 adds an impossible condition. Only if the heavens can be measured and the earth's foundations explored to the bottom will God "cast off all the seed of Israel for all that they have done."
Notice "for all that they have done." God is not ignoring Israel's sins. He is declaring that even those sins will not end His commitment.
The plain referent here is the seed of Israel. Christians may rejoice that the covenant blesses others through Christ, but should not read Israel out of a promise made explicitly to Israel.

Jeremiah instructs Baruch with the Lord's words: put the deeds "in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days." Clay jars protected documents over long periods. Much later, scrolls stored in jars near the Dead Sea survived for many centuries. The instruction expects a long wait; Jeremiah had spoken of seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10).

runs.text: Verse 15 explains the sign: "Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land." This was a commanded prophetic sign, not general advice to invest boldly in failing markets or ignore prudence. It declared God's future.
As application, Paul's "treasure in earthen vessels" (
2 Corinthians 4:7
) suggests that fragile containers can carry lasting promises.

What promises from God are you "storing" for a future you cannot yet see?

Zedekiah admits the real obstacle: "I am afraid of the Jews that are fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they deliver me into their hand, and they mock me." He fears humiliation from his own countrymen who had already surrendered. "The fear of man bringeth a snare" (Proverbs 29:25).

runs.text: Jeremiah answers gently: "They shall not deliver thee. Obey, I beseech thee, the voice of the LORD… so it shall be well unto thee, and thy soul shall live." Whose opinion do you most fear when obeying God? How could you face that fear?
